A positive test is a clue, not the final answer.

Actual tells us whether a person really has flu; the test predicts positive (+) or negative (−). Even an accurate test can produce many false alarms when flu is rare.

evidence.name: basics
evidence.text:
A test’s accuracy on sick people is not your chance of being sick.

When you get a Test +, you don’t know whether you came from the sick group or the healthy group. Right now, out of 1,000 people, 100 have the flu (yielding 62 true catches) and 900 are healthy (yielding 0 false alarms). Your actual chance of having the flu is 62 out of all 62 positive tests (100%).

evidence.text:
Same top number (TP), different bottom group: why TPR ≠ Precision

Look at TPR and Precision below: both have the exact same top number (TP = sick people caught)! The only difference is who you divide by. TPR divides horizontally by all sick people (top row), while Precision divides vertically by all positive tests (right column, which mixes sick catches with healthy false alarms). evidence.name: bayes
evidence.text:
Bayes’ theorem in 3 natural steps: from 1,000 people to your chance of flu

The easiest way to understand Bayes’ theorem is with 1,000 people: first split them by how common flu is (p = 10%), next count how many from each row get a Test +, and finally take the sick share of all positive tests (P(flu | test +)).

Why the 1,000-person count formula equals Bayes’ formula

The vertical bar | means “given” (which group we restrict our attention to). Because TP = 1,000 × TPR × p and FP = 1,000 × FPR × (1 − p), the population size 1,000 cancels out from top and bottom—turning expected counts into Bayes’ exact rate formula for P(flu | test +).

0.62 × 0.1 ÷ [0.62 × 0.1 + 0 × 0.9] = 100%

Positive Likelihood Ratio (LR+ = TPR ÷ FPR): ∞ (0 false alarms). Dividing TP by FP gives Posterior Odds = LR+ × Prior Odds.

1. CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY (BAYES’ RULE)
P(A | B) =
P(B | A) × P(A)
P(B | A) × P(A) + P(B | not A) × P(not A)
2. CANCEL N = 1,000 FROM TP ÷ (TP + FP)

TPR × p
TPR × p + FPR × (1 − p)
